tagline.text: A one-hour boat ride to Batangas' hidden emerald sea

items.credit: Ralff Nestor Nacor / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons
Ralff Nestor Nacor / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A white sand beach on the south side of Marikaban Island in Tingloy, off the coast of Anilao. Clear emerald water and coral at the rocky end of the beach make for great snorkeling, and it's a great-value island getaway you can reach in a day from Manila by bus and boat.
Masasa Beach lies in the village of San Juan on the south side of Marikaban Island, the main island of Tingloy, Batangas province's only island municipality. It's reached by a
45-minute–1-hour

boat ride south across the water from the Anilao peninsula in Mabini. Behind it rises a palm-covered hill, and in front the sea shifts from jade to deep blue with the depth of the water, giving a "real island sea" look rarely seen this close to Manila.

The beach consists of several hundred meters of white-to-cream sand, with a stretch of black rock and coral at the western end. The water off the sand is shallow and calm, good for swimming, and toward the rocky stretch, tropical fish gather among the coral, so you can snorkel right off the beach. Some travelers have even spotted sea turtles if they're lucky.
Masasa became known through word of mouth in the early 2010s, and campers once flocked here in such numbers that trash and noise became serious problems. So starting in

, the Tingloy government banned overnight camping on the beach and introduced an environmental fee and a trash deposit system. Now the beach is enjoyed during the day, with overnight guests staying at village homestays. As a result, the village has kept its simple fishing-village feel without any large resorts.

The trip takes a little effort, switching between bus, jeepney, boat, and tricycle in turn, but that's what keeps the cost low for such clear water. It's recommended for backpackers, friends who love snorkeling, and travelers who prefer a simple island village to a flashy resort. Pair it with diving in Anilao for a full taste of Batangas' seas.
On calm days, the water off the beach is so clear you can see straight to the bottom. The color is most vivid in the morning sun, so it's worth arriving early.
The rocks and coral at the western end of the beach hold plenty of fish. Gear can be rented on the beach for about
per person; float rather than stand to avoid stepping on the coral.
A roughly
2-hour
route up to a rock outcrop whose name means "married couple rock," manageable even for beginners. From the top, you get a 360-degree view over all of Marikaban Island and the surrounding sea.
A boat tour from Masasa around Sepok Point, Tawil Point, Oscar Beach, and a small lagoon. It's a chance to see coastal cliffs, hidden beaches, and snorkeling spots all in one trip.
A small, uninhabited island shaped like a Mexican hat, often included on island-hopping routes. Entrance runs about
, and the snorkeling around the island is good.

blocks.title: Sunset on the beach and homestay evenings

children.text: In the afternoon, once the day-trippers have left, the beach turns quiet, and the sunset colors the hills of Marikaban Island. Staying at a homestay lets you have this time, and the early-morning sea, all to yourself.

blocks.title: The Anilao coast from the boat

children.text: On the boat crossing from Anilao to Tingloy, you'll pass the Mabini coastline lined with dive resorts and a scatter of large and small islands. On a clear day, you can even see the mountains of Mindoro Island in the distance.

At the port, pay the environmental fee and board a public boat to Tingloy (check the boat schedule)
Arrive in Tingloy, take a tricycle to Masasa Beach
Swim and snorkel the rocky stretch
Seafood lunch at a beach shop or homestay
A short island-hopping trip, or rest on the beach

Boat from Anilao to Tingloy, check in at your homestay
Swim and snorkel at the beach, island hopping to Sombrero Island and Sepok Point

The departure port changes with the season. Generally, in the dry season when the northeast monsoon blows, Anilao Port is used, and in the rainy season, when the southwest monsoon blows, Talaga Port, about
3km
to the south, is used to avoid the waves. The timing of the switch varies each year, so check the Mabini tourism office's notices before you leave.
At the port you'll pay an environmental fee of about
, a terminal fee, and a trash deposit of about
, refunded on your return. The amounts and the system may change, so check the latest notice.

If you're in a large group, you can also charter a boat straight from Anilao to Masasa. For about 10 people, a boat runs about
Take the SLEX–STAR Tollway toward Batangas City, then go via Bauan to Anilao Port or Talaga Port in Mabini, which takes about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours 30 minutes
. You leave the car at a private parking lot around the port for about

From Tingloy port to Masasa Beach takes about
15–20 minutes
by tricycle, for about
. It helps to agree on a pickup time with the driver in advance for the return trip.
Since Masasa's whole appeal is the color of the water, go on a sunny day.
November–May
is the best window, and within that,
March–May
has the calmest seas and clearest water, ideal for snorkeling. That said, weekends and Holy Week in this period draw large crowds of day-trippers, so weekdays are recommended. During
December–February
, the northeast monsoon can occasionally make the Anilao–Tingloy boat crossing rough.
During the
June–October

rainy season, the southwest monsoon blows straight into Marikaban Island's south coast, raising waves and clouding the water. When a typhoon warning is issued, the coast guard suspends public boat service, so you could get stranded on the island. During this period, be sure to check the weather and boat schedule on the morning of your trip. Midday temperatures run around
year-round, so sun protection matters regardless of season.

There are no large resorts at Masasa Beach — homestays run by villagers behind the beach are the only lodging. Most offer fan rooms or simple air-conditioned rooms with a shared bathroom, at about

per person. Overnight camping is banned, so if you want to stay the night, book a homestay in advance. If you'd rather have more comfortable facilities, stay at a dive resort on the Anilao mainland and visit Masasa as a day trip.

The beach has a handful of small shops and simple eateries selling instant noodles, drinks, and simple rice meals, but the choices are limited. Ask at your homestay and they may grill the day's catch for you, or cook it as sinigang, a sour soup. It's a good idea to bring water, snacks, and fruit from Batangas City or Mabini in advance, and on the way back, round off the trip with Batangas lomi, bulalo, and kapeng barako.
For a day trip, take the earliest bus out of Manila so you have plenty of time on the beach. Check the last return boat time first, before anything else.
Collect your trash in the bag given at the port and show it on your way back to get your deposit refunded.
Power on the island sometimes cuts out late at night, and outages are common. Bring a power bank and a flashlight.
There are almost no ATMs on the island, so withdraw the cash you'll need in Batangas City or Mabini beforehand. Bringing plenty of small bills helps too.
Mobile data generally works on the beach, but signal strength can vary by carrier. Save your homestay's contact number in advance.
Bringing your own snorkel gear, aqua shoes, and a dry bag saves on rental fees and makes getting on and off the boat easier.
Day-use tents (sunshades) are allowed but must come down in the evening. Beach rules can change, so check the posted signs when you arrive.
At Anilao Port you have to pay the boat fare, environmental fee, terminal fee, and garbage deposit all at once, so having about
per person ready in small-denomination cash makes the line move faster.

Overnight camping is banned on Masasa Beach. If you plan to stay the night, book a homestay, and also be prepared for the chance of getting stuck on the island overnight if bad weather halts the boats.
There's no lifeguard on the beach. The water gets deep quickly just past the rocky area and there are currents, so wear a life vest and snorkel with a buddy.
It's easy to cut your feet on coral and rocks or get stung by a sea urchin. Wear aqua shoes, and don't step on or touch the coral.
Public boats check life vests and passenger counts to avoid overloading. Don't board a private boat that insists on sailing on a high-wave day.
There's little shade on the beach. Bring a hat, a rash guard, reef-safe sunscreen, and plenty of water.
This is a quiet village where people live. Avoid loud late-night drinking and loud music.
